Epilogue: Interpretation—Then and Now: If, When, and How

Eva Papiasvili Ph.D., ABPP

Eva Papiasvili

Eva Papiasvili  

As we come to the end of the issue, it is important to remind ourselves that it is in the spirit of open-ended creative inquiry of the psychoanalytic interpretation, as well as in the context of this publication, that the dialectics of endings and beginings unfold: Each ending contains a potential for a new beginning.

Inherently, people of any age and circumstance engage perpetually in interpreting. It is via ubiquitous process of multiply interpreting ourselves within ourselves and with (and sometimes without) others, that we survive, adapt, and create. Creative interpretation and insight of the founder of psychoanalysis marked the birth of the field. Today, the multiple dimensions of the interpretative process, as presented on the preceding pages, may be an exploratory meeting place of a rich dialogue not only between two participants of the psychoanalytic inquiry in clinical situation, but also an exploratory meeting place of the various schools of thought and research. Through the ongoing study of various dimensions and processes participating in the interpretation, the sometimes disconnected plurality of parent theories may be thus transformed into a generation of hybrid internally connectable (interpenetratable) interpretative approaches of a wide open arsenal, to effect a continuous process of creative recovery of disconnected disparities, within our patients, within our theories and within ourselves.

As a guest editor, I express gratitude to the Editor-in-Chief, Dr. Joseph Lichtenberg, for his inspirational vision for this issue and making the journal of Psychoanalytic Inquiry available as a forum for the fruitful international exchange of views on the subject of interpretation. My heartfelt thanks are also to the Associate Editor, Dr. Carol Levin, for her logistical support with a human touch and many words of encouragement throughout the process of the creation of this special issue. Additionally, I would never be able to accomplish all of the ad hoc translation of original passages, editing, and organizational work involved in putting together an international issue such as this without a devoted and competent assistant, a doctoral student of mine, Ms. Emily Lyman, M.A.

Introduction

Masahisa Nishizono M.D., Ph.D.

Masahisa Nishizono

Masahisa Nishizono   Masahisa Nishizono is a Former President of the Japan Psychoanalytical Society.Contact Masahisa Nishizono, M.D., Ph.D. ZVA11061@nifty.com 6-3-21, Likura, Sawara-ku, Fukuoka-shi, 814-0161, Japan.

2014 marked the 75th anniversary of the death of Sigmund Freud. In the last three-quarters of a century since then, psychoanalysis has crossed Europe and spread all over the world. It continues to develop and expand. However, it does not operate under a single, uniform doctrine. In the United States, ego psychology had a overwhelming influence on psychoanalysis in the post-WW2 world, but today, self-psychology and relational psychoanalysis are also flourishing. In France, Lacanian psychoanalysis remains influential. The International Psychoanalytical Association held a meeting to commemorate its 100th anniversary not in a European city, but in Beijing, China. It appears that their intentions were not merely to help psychoanalysis grow and spread in Asian countries, but also bring it into contact with the origins and characteristics of Asian cultures. We are currently living in an age of mutual understanding and symbolic relationships. In this sense, it is highly significant that Psychoanalytic Inquiry has published a special issue on Japan.

Japan was the first country in Asia to embrace so-called modernization. The political systems and academic disciplines of Europe and the United States were brought into Japan, and many were formally adopted. The introduction of publications on psychoanalysis was no exception. It appears that books by Sigmund Freud were already being studied in 1912. Later, psychoanalytic treatment also began. In those days, however, psychoanalytic practitioners had not always undergone sufficient training as psychoanalysts. A number of pioneers who lamented to this flaw visited Vienna, underwent training, albeit briefly, and then returned to Japan to perform psychoanalytic treatment. These individuals comprised Japan’s first generation of psychoanalysis. One of their leading figures was Dr. Heisaku Kosawa, who trained and natured the second generation of psychoanalysts, whom I describe next.

After the Second World War, laws and established social systems were changed in Japan, and values upheld by society and families were altered. Faced with these changes, many neurotic patients sought psychiatric treatment. This led to heightened interest in psychotherapy and psychoanalysis on the part of the country’s psychiatrists. It was under these circumstances that Kosawa established two organizations: the Japan Psychoanalytic Society, which trains and fosters psychoanalysts; and the Japan Psychoanalytical Association, the goal of which is to spread psychodynamic psychotherapy among psychiatrists and clinical psychologists. A number of prominent individuals appeared, including Dr. Takeo Doi, who was renowned worldwide for his amae theory. Another was Dr. Keigo Okonogi, who complemented Kosawa’s Ajase complex. These individuals were Japan’s second generation of psychoanalysts. Their academic approach was characterized by their emphasis on mother-child relationships in personality formation and in therapeutic situations.

Encounter with Psychoanalysis: How I Became a Psychoanalyst

Takayuki Kinugasa MD

Takayuki Kinugasa

Takayuki Kinugasa   Dr. Kinugasa is Director, Hiroshima-City Mental Health and Welfare Center; and Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry, Hiroshima University. He retired last year and is working privately.CONTACT Takayuki Kinugasa, M.D. t-kinugasa@ab.cyberhome.ne.jp Heiwa-Ohdori Mental Clinic, 8-6, Fujita Bldg. 3F, Kakamachi, Naka-ku, Hiroshima-shi, 732-0037, Japan.

I encountered psychoanalysis for the first time in my registrar time, when I treated some borderline patients and read borderline papers by Dr. Kernberg. Later, I studied psychoanalytic clinical practice at The Tavistock Clinic in London. This greatly influenced me to choose to be a psychoanalyst.

When I was 10, I was involved in a severe traffic accident and was hospitalized. I met many victims and survivors of the atomic bomb there. All of them were suffering from heavy mental trauma. My father himself was harmed in the atomic bomb attack, and he also survived but suffered from profound mental pain and agony through his life. I show that these experiences were influential background for my understanding the importance of psychoanalysis.

Confrontation and the Fool’s Method

Henry Smith MD

Henry Smith

Henry Smith   Henry F. Smith, M.D., is the former Editor of The Psychoanalytic Quarterly.CONTACT Henry F. Smith, M.D. henryfsmith@gmail.com 17 Hammond Street, Cambridge, MA 02138.

The history of the term confrontation is reviewed. It is suggested that the reason it was so difficult to define the term over the years is that it is fundamentally an interactive term, imported into an era in which many analysts behaved as if there were no interaction—or should be none. Contemporary analytic process can be seen as a series of confrontations between two people by virtue of the intrinsic differences between them. Three clinical vignettes illustrate this point and its implications. A final section of the article examines the dialogue between the Fool and King Lear in Shakespeare’s (1606) play, which allows consideration of the complex nature of confrontation and other aspects of therapeutic dialogue often neglected.

Prologue: Psychoanalytic Reflections on a Critical Question: Are We a Culture That Glorifies Violence?

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein   CONTACT Melvin Bornstein, M.D. melvinbornstein@gmail.com 625 Purdy Street, Birmingham, MI 48009.

The title of this issue, “Psychoanalytic Reflections on a Critical Question: Are We a Culture That Glorifies Violence?”, evolved from the editor’s initial consideration of what is unique that psychoanalysis can contribute to the understanding and reduction of violence in the United States. The contributors of this issue have referred to statistics of the very high incidence of violence in the United States. They have referred to the historical roots of violence in the United States beginning with a Revolution, the killing and dislodging American Indians from their land and damaging their culture, the initiation and upholding of slavery with its aftermath by treating Blacks as they were not human, the gun-slinging individualism of the West, and the grandiosity of its military power. Each of these happenings have contributed to the exulted, violent image of the United States. All the contributors have pointed to the vast social and cultural literature devoted to violence, its causes, and its remedies in the United States.

With this beginning, all the writers use a psychoanalytic perspective that enables them to focus on the inner lives of their subjects, who are continually shifting their emotional attention between looking at an outward reality and an inward state filled with memories and fantasies. Focusing outwardly is more difficult. It involves pain, vulnerability, thinking, organizing, and adapting while focusing inwardly is immediate, safer, and temporarily gratifying. Each contributor emphasizes the human capacity to communicate with language and to create narratives and meaning to deal with the inside and the outside worlds. Communication enables emotional growth and greater strength to keep a focus on reality.

Each contributor implies the presence of a powerful force to repeat, rather than endure, the feelings and vulnerability of the past while feeling alive in the present with vitality and love.

Elisabeth Waugaman emphasizes that within a society that is immersed in the glorification of violence there is a lack of adequate communication that would promote an increase in understanding adaptation and safety.

Understanding America’s Obsession with Guns: How Did We Get Where We Are?

Elisabeth Waugaman PHD

Elisabeth Waugaman

Elisabeth Waugaman   Elisabeth Waugaman, Ph.D., is Faculty, New Directions (Writing Program), Washington Center for Psychoanalysis, Washington, D.C.CONTACT Elisabeth Waugaman, Ph.D. elisabethw@comcast.net 8109 Horseshoe Lane, Potomac, MD 20854.

This article is the result of my attempts to dialogue with gun advocates beginning with blogs about gun control for Psychology Today Online in 2012, after the Aurora shootings. A review of American history and popular culture in film provides insights into why so many Americans distrust national government, why there is so much fear of “the other,” why there is so much anger, and why Americans are so obsessed with guns. The Revolutionary War and the Civil War created an inherent suspicion of government that still persists, and the country evolved an ongoing fear of the other beginning with Native Americans and slavery, which has continued with fear of the Mafia after WWI, fear of communists after WWII, fear of Muslims after 9/11, and fear of “illegal aliens” after the most recent recession. American film developed while the country was still fighting Native Americans. The industry was influenced by war documentaries and strains to maintain audiences with ever-increasing violence and special effects. Creating a dialogue with gun advocates requires maintaining clear boundaries and constant awareness of historical and cultural fears, myth, repression, splitting, and narcissism.

The articles written from a psychoanalytic perspective deepen the understanding of the enormous problem of violence and its glorification in our culture and what can be done about it. By focusing on what is taking place inside the minds of people and groups of people who contribute to violence and its glorification, greater understanding and repair become available.

The importance of quality and quantity of communication and relatedness from all levels of consciousness and unconsciousness (Lothane, Waugaman, Nissim-Sabat, Summers, Twemlow, Nayar-Akhtar).

The shifting dynamics that reverberate within the person because of “restrictions of options” (Nissim-Sabat) that are not only present in culture, but have been internalized and effect the responses to current actual restrictions of options because of the difficulty in transforming repetitions into narratives.

The shifting dynamics also applies to the grandiosity and idealization of being a North American (Summers), which is defensive against narcissistic injuries because at one time they appeared impossible to live with.

Without an appreciation of altruism and cooperation as a fundamental motivation, possibilities of change are often time missed (Twemlow).

We have a growing literature on the application of psychoanalytic knowledge in the community. Psychoanalytic Inquiry devoted an entire issue to psychoanalysts in the trenches (“The Community Analyst in Troubled Waters,” 2012, Volume 32[2]) that demonstrates how useful psychoanalytic understanding can be when applied in the community.

Classical psychoanalytic tradition reinforced the idea that the patient use free association and the analyst was similarly limited to a rule of free-floating attention (listening) leading to interpretation of unconscious trends. The central aim of technique was to ensure that transference of the past onto the analyst would occur in a context that could permit interpretations of the transference. This article examines ways in which therapists use psychoanalytic theory to distance themselves from the relational aspect of the therapeutic dyad. The use of the therapists’ use of a professional self as a protective and distancing in the course of an analysis or therapy tends to derail the development of a successful therapeutic engagement.

Analysts need to be aware that each word used by a patient is composed of a constant conjunction of a person’s intimate emotional and historical referents, conscious and unconscious affects, memories, and conceptions and fantasies. In this article, I share a vignette from a long-term analysis, illustrating my experience during the scene and the clinical decisions that I make both in and out of my awareness. The vignette is notable for strong affect, as well as intense and surprising imagery and words. What is also notable is that this scene rings true. This article is equal parts a demonstration of pretheoretical moments of clinical decision-making and a discussion of clinical epistemology. I examine what it means when something rings true, explain the value of holding certainty and ambiguity in a dialectic tension, and describe conditions under which we may trust the ring of truth in clinical situations. Finally, I show how I find my way to psychoanalytic faith in this clinical example, as I experience an informed surrender to the psychoanalytic process.

Tetsuro Takahashi M.D., Ph.D.

Tetsuro Takahashi

Tetsuro Takahashi   Dr. Takahashi is a member of American Psychoanalytic Society, and honorary member of Japan Psychoanalytic Society. After retiring from Training and Supervising Analyst of Japan Psychoanalytic Society, now he lives in Tigard, Oregon.CONTACT Tetsuro Takahashi, M.D., Ph.D. Takatetu111332@gmail.com 10370 S. W. Hoodview Drive, Tigard, OR 97224.

Commentary

This article is based on a special lecture at the annual meeting of Japan Psychoanalytical Society, 2013, which meant Dr. Takahashi’s retirement from his professional career in Japan. In brief, Dr. Takahashi started his career as a psychiatrist in Tokyo University Hospital, who then became interested in Child Psychiatry and got acquainted with Dr. Ogura, who returned from the United States after working and training for eight years there, mainly at Menninger Clinic. This encounter stimulated Dr. Takahashi to head for the West, for further training as a child psychiatrist. Different from his original idea of learning for two years, his stay in the United States extended more than a quarter century and, once he settled down in Topeka, saw him as the director of The Hope Program at the Menninger Clinic helping adults with complex psychiatric issues. Then his quest progressed to having formal psychoanalytic training at the Topeka Institute for Psychoanalysis.

On being qualified in his middle sixties, and his having completed identification as a psychoanalyst, Dr. Takahashi decided to return to the East, this time to provide his experience and knowledge to Japanese colleagues, at Osaka, Japan. After seventeen years of teaching and clinical work in Japan, he remarked that this lecture was his farewell speech, which consisted of two parts; first, as in Japan, once-a-week psychoanalytic psychotherapy has been broadly performed, so that he had to invent a way to organize and facilitate training methods, specific for psychoanalytic psychotherapy; and, second, to overcome and resolve his quest and the reason behind it, he needed to narrate his professional pilgrimage to a Japanese audience, who also seek the truth in the human psyche.

Epilogue: Psychoanalytic Work with the Dreams of Children: The Forgotten Royal Road

Christine Anzieu-Premmereur M.D., Ph.D. , Denia Barrett MSW and Ruth Karush MD

Ruth Karush

Ruth Karush  

Freud addressed himself to the topic children’s dreams in both The Interpretation of Dreams and in his Introductory Lectures (Lecture VIII, 1915-1916). In his later remarks on the subject, he noted that dreams in early childhood, from the beginning of observable mental activity to the fourth or fifth year, are relatively undistorted wish-fulfillment ones that allowed him to “draw conclusions with great ease and certainty on the essential nature of dreams in general” (p. 126). He asserted no analytic methods were necessary to understand these dreams, as long as one has some knowledge of the child’s experience the preceding day; the dream is a reaction to “some regret, longing or wish that has not been dealt with.” He further believed that such infantile dreams are not confined to early life, but may occur throughout childhood and even in adulthood under certain conditions. In this lecture, he relates the dreams of two family members, each of whom had an illness that obliged her to go without food the day before. The 19-month-old girl dreamed: “Anna F., stwawbewwies, wild stwawbewwies, omblet, pudden!” Her grandmother dreamed she, herself, had been served the most appetizing delicacies. Freud argued against those who took the point of view that children’s dreams are without meaning, saying they are “intelligible, completely valid mental acts” and put this forth as reinforcement for his hypothesis that the dreams of adults are not “mere twitchings” either (pp. 126–132).

Freud (1915-1916) recognized that dream distortion could be observed in the dreams of children by the age of five. Unlike the dreams of younger children, such dreams do require psychoanalytic technique to be understood, just like the more complex dreams of adults. “They must be interpreted—that is translated—and their manifest content replaced by their latent one” (p. 135).

It has been almost a century since Freud delivered this lecture, and some of the same questions about children’s dreams remain in the minds of neuroscientists and psychoanalysts alike. We are grateful for the contribution on dream science and theory from Soudabeh Givrad, for the many clinical examples representing the dreams of children from prelatency through adolescence, and for the thoughtful discussions that make up this issue. As we said in our prologue, our intention was to bring together the experiences of a number of child psychoanalysts to share how work with the dreams of their young patients offered a beneficial and pleasurable means to enrich the mutual understanding of both analytic partners. When asked to be a discussant, one analyst initially reflected that she did not think dreams had figured so prominently in her work—only to have a child report a dream to her almost immediately afterwards. We believe this illustrates the point that our own interest and attentiveness to the dreams of our child and adolescent patients is a necessary condition for traveling, not detouring from, the royal road. We hope others will be encouraged to include work with dreams when they write or present case material. Perhaps someone will write about dreams that the child or adolescent psychoanalyst has about young patients. Those who treat only adults may perhaps become more attuned and tell us when their patients report dreams 269

Epilogue: The Clinical Experience of Time

Henry Smith MD

Henry Smith

Henry Smith   CONTACT Henry F. Smith, M.D.henryfsmith@gmail.com 17 Hammond Street, Cambridge, MA 02138.

Perhaps the complexity of writing about time is reflected in the unique approaches each of our eight authors brings to the subject. For an issue on a single topic, there is remarkably little redundancy from one article to another, either in demonstrable theory or clinical practice. This is the more surprising because the authors were not chosen primarily for their diversity, and the variation that results is not the all-too-predictable one, based on a selection of analysts from different schools, but rather one that bespeaks each analyst’s individual approach and so is a valuable reflection of the disparate ways analysts actually think and go about their work.

Donald Moss opens the issue and begins his article with an incisive explication of the baby’s experience of time at the beginning of life, struggling to capture, in fantasy, the satisfaction once provided by the Other, now frustrated by delay. Thus begins the child’s first encounter with what Freud (1900) called “the bitter experience of life” (p. 566) and the failures of secondary as opposed to primary process wish fulfillment. Along the way, Moss speaks for the complexity of time itself and the difficulty we have of living in the present, suffering as we do a kind of death with the “ongoing loss of every present moment” (p. 359). And, conversely, he speaks to our attempts to simplify time with a fetishistic focus on the here and now, as if it could be detached from the there and then. Ultimately, both parties in the analytic room must find their way into the three dimensions of time. These are themes that are elaborated by all of our authors in their own characteristic ways.

Thus, Alessandra Lemma, too, describes the experience of time at birth, but the birth she is describing is that of a transgendered patient whose trajectory in time was interrupted by hormones and surgery and so is disconnected from a past that she disavows. Her experience of time begins with a hormonal and surgical rebirth, and so she is living in a surgically engineered present with a surgically excised past. This creates some fundamental difficulties in thinking because, as Lemma points out, it is impossible to think without a past and without a concept of “before-me-ness” (p. 362).

On Becoming a Psychoanalyst in Japan

Akiyoshi Okada M.D., Ph.D.

Akiyoshi Okada

Akiyoshi Okada   Dr. Okada is a psychoanalyst from the Japan Psychoanalytical Society.CONTACT Akiyoshi Okada, M.D., Ph.D. Psychoanal2010@yahoo.co.jp Faculty of Humanities, Nanzan University, 18 Yamasato-Machi, Showa-ku, Nagoya, 466-8784, Japan.

This special issue introduces psychoanalysis in Japan, its history, thoughts, and development, through the autobiographies of some Japanese psychoanalysts. I graduated relatively recently from a training course in psychoanalysis at the Japan Institute of Psychoanalysis and was certified as a psychoanalyst by the Japan Psychoanalytic Society (JPS). If I am to write about why I aimed to become a psychoanalyst in Japan and how I became one, not only my personal history but also the influences of Japanese culture and Japanese therapeutic culture will undoubtedly be important. In this article, by relating my life history, I trace the path I followed for becoming a psychoanalyst and explore the broader implications of my experience. The paper “An Autobiographical Study” by Freud (1925) is a famous autobiographical psychoanalytic essay, and a more recent paper “Learning from Life―Becoming a Psychoanalyst” by Casement (2006) is also well known. To publicize an autobiography, a psychoanalyst always includes the possibility of self-disclosure. Because I am still practicing psychoanalysis regularly, I hesitate slightly to write this article. However, writing an autobiography is also, in part, a process of self-analysis after becoming a psychoanalyst, and can be considered a part of a psychoanalyst’s interminable training (Okada, 2012).

Lucy LaFarge MD

Lucy LaFarge

Lucy LaFarge   Lucy LaFarge, M.D., is the Editor for North America, The International Journal of Psychoanalysis; Training and Supervising Analyst, Columbia University Psychoanalytic Center; and Professor of Psychiatry, Weill Cornell Medical College.CONTACT Lucy LaFarge, M.D. llafarge@verizon.net 239 Central Park West, Suite 1-BE, New York, NY 10024.

In the broadest sense, the term confrontation describes an interaction in which persons are brought together to elicit truth—an encounter central to all analytic work. Within the psychoanalytic literature, the term has generally been defined according to the theoretical assumptions of classical ego psychology and has referred to an interaction in which an objective, observing analyst confronts the patient with aspects of himself that the analyst sees and the patient does not, leading the patient to see first his wish not to know and then the unknown part of himself—the stranger within. In newer, intersubjective models, confrontation continues to be an essential interaction in analytic work, but it takes a different form. As the analyst comes to know the patient, the patient’s confrontation with the analyst’s separate subjectivity—with the stranger without—leads for the patient to a confrontation with his fantasies of becoming known to another and, ultimately, to other unconscious aspects of his inner world. An extended clinical example illustrates this technical approach and its yield and points to potential problems that may be associated with it.

In this article, I, a Japanese psychoanalyst, describe the various twists and turns I went through to reach psychoanalysis in the process of seeking the truth as well as what I experienced through psychoanalysis. Although this is a personal story, it indicates that there is a truth beyond cultural differences that cannot be reached without psychoanalysis. I learned the method of phenomenological psychopathology from Professor Tatossian in France and tried to come closer to the essential nature of the mind. However, I came across the thought of Jacques Lacan there and was fascinated. I also came to know the importance of Freud and Klein through Lacan. I received individual psychoanalysis from Dr. Doi, Dr. Kinugasa, and Miss Betty Joseph because I wanted to understand psychoanalysis. Although it was a short period, I was greatly influenced by my psychoanalysis experience with Miss Joseph. I present a part of the sessions and demonstrate that a direct contact with the alive unconscious phantasy in the here and now was pursued there. This experience was something that brought about not only liveliness, but also elements of anxiety and madness to my subsequent life. I state that the work of psychoanalysts is to always call into question one’s own blind spots and even your own existence, by being engaged in the movement of the living unconsciousness that appears in the here and now.

Prologue: The Clinical Experience of Time

Henry Smith MD

Henry Smith

Henry Smith   CONTACT Henry F. Smith, M.D. henryfsmith@gmail.com 17 Hammond Street, Cambridge, MA 02138.

Beginning with Freud’s intermittent notes on the timelessness of the unconscious, the rhetoric among psychoanalysts on the subject of time has favored abstract general concepts over the specifically clinical experience of time—this, despite the fact that the latter, one could argue, is at the heart of our work. Under the clinical experience of time, we might include such items as the patient’s experience of time, the analyst’s experience of time, the nature of analytic time itself, and the clinical experience of what Freud called timelessness.

Time does appear as a factor in our literature on technique. Traditionally, analysts focused on the history of the patient and the reconstruction of the past. More recently, we have been enjoined to ignore all that and to consider only the present moment (Bion, 1967). And sometimes we are prompted to allow an image of the patient’s future (Loewald, 1956). These directives provide complex dilemmas for the analyst’s experience of time, inviting and sometimes demanding a specific temporal focus that runs counter to what we might think of as a free-floating experience of time.

If the latter might be considered a version of timelessness, akin to the experience of evenly hovering attention, this is not universally how the term timeless is used. Sometimes it refers, as here, to a release from the demands of time, sometimes to time’s unchanging tyranny, and sometimes to a landscape over which time has no dominion whatsoever. You will find these and other meanings in the articles that follow, as we ask eight authors, each with his or her own point of view, to consider the clinical experience of time.

Drawing on sharply conceived clinical vignettes, Donald Moss begins our issue with the implications of the shift in infancy from primary to secondary process functioning and from immediacy to delay. For Moss, timelessness refers to the primary process state in which “wish is satisfied immediately” (p. 352) before the “bitter experience” (p. 352) of delay forces a reevaluation of one’s objects. Thus every relation to an object is simultaneously a relation to time, and patients who “retreat from objects are faced with the more daunting problem of having to retreat from time itself” (p. 351). Although the painful acceptance of present time is something we all avoid, analytic work cannot take place unless all three dimensions of time—past, present, and future—are in play for both analyst and patient.

Albert Schwietzer (reported in Cousins, 1979) was asked how he could account for the fact that anyone could believe they will get better after treatment with a witch doctor. He responded by saying,

The witch doctor succeeds for the same reason that all of us (doctors) succeed. Each patient carries his own doctor inside of him. They come to us not knowing that truth. We are at our best when we give the doctor who resides within each patient a chance to go to work. [Cousins, 1979, pp. 68–69]

Images and imagination appear to rest delicately upon such a foundation. In many ways, each of the articles presented here speaks to a subtle interaction of science and mystery. For while the articles of this issue do take us closer to understanding some of the experiential, theoretical and clinical workings of image-based experience, we are, inevitably, left with more wonder than scientific certainty. Bachelard (1968) spoke to this when he stated,

One can study only what one has first dreamed about. Science is formed rather on a reverie than on an experiment, and it takes a good many experiments to dispel the mists of the dream. [p. 22]

With deep appreciation to each of the authors, we bring this issue to a close.

The editorial intent of this issue was to ask: What, before you apply theory, do you do? What responses establish comfort or discomfort with what you do? What do you do next? And each contributor, with deep reflection and great courage, has found a way to make those questions her or his own.

Any analytic reader with an interest in the evolution and clinical application of contemporary theory will be familiar with Henry Smith, Frank Summers, and Fred Busch. Yet each of these authors found a way—while using concepts as means of communication—to provide (through vicarious introspection) to sit with him as he sits with a patient.

Henry Smith questions our preference “to think [that we plan our] clinical decisions consciously and deliberately” (p. 527) and frames his contribution in the context of enactment. In a detailed clinical vignette centering on a transference interpretation involving a patient’s dream of being chased, Smith makes clear: “I am an active participant in that scenario. In the very persistence of my efforts to facilitate her putting her fantasies into words, I am, in fact, chasing her and cannot not chase her with my own words” (p. 529). He goes on to describe and explore a dialectical process in both patient and analyst—functioning without regard to a specific orientation—of insight and action, each moving away from and yet provoking the other.

Frank Summers calls explicitly on the concept of a dialectical process, “for the analytic therapist [whose] life is lived on the precipice of the various possible intervention categories” (p. 538). Each choice of perception and intervention rules another choice. Summers describes his clinical back-and-forth between listening to associations, noting connections and patterns and the feeling of a gap in the affective relationship which leads him to intervene in the service of a shared feeling of connection. Within the dialectic, he states and demonstrates his priority. “I make my clinical decisions on the basis of what has the greatest transformative potential” (p. 546). And even while recognizing the importance of exploration of the transference, “the principle of affective resonance trumps reference to the analytic relationship” (p. 546).

Lester Lenoff LCSW

Lester Lenoff

Lester Lenoff   CONTACT Lester Lenoff, LCSW lstrlenoff@gmail.com 150 East 57th Street, Apt. 24AB, New York, NY 10022.

The analysts who contributed to this issue can, for purposes of comparison, be divided into two groups—those who begin at a presumption of a dialectic between two equally valid forms of clinical listening response and those who begin with a single priority. On the basis the word and spirit of what they have written (and personal contact I have had with a number of these analysts), neither group would ignore the relevance of the other’s concerns; it is matter of starting point.

Henry Smith and Frank Summers both begin with an inevitable dialectic. There are two vantages from which the analyst can listen to and respond to the patient. Each is equally valuable as the other. But you can’t do both at once. And each of their articles opens the author up to the reader as to how he negotiates his listening, his response or restraint, and his sense of clinical direction.

Henry Smith sees his dilemma arising within a moment-by-moment enactment. With his patient he offers a “straightforward, even classical” (p. 528) interpretation that she both elicits and fears his analytic pursuit of her. The patient initially withdraws, but then responds, again in a straightforward manner by associating more deeply into the meaning this has for her. Yet Smith, in retrospect, recognizes that despite the ostensible neutrality and anonymity of his interpretation, he “cannot not chase her with my own words” (p. 529). And he notes that each analytic orientation, in raising its own privileged clinical stance to the status of technique, has lost sight of the analyst’s enacted participation in what emerges.

For Frank Summers, there is no mode of analytic responsiveness that does require temporary suspension of another equally legitimate (at another moment) mode of responding. He documents this dialectic between moments of more restrained listening and reflection on the transference and countertransference and moments of a shared feeling of connection. Summers states, and it bears restating, that in seeking the “greatest transformative potential … the principle of affective resonance trumps reference to the analytic relationship” (p. 546).

Prologue: Images in Mind: Working with Image-based Experience in Psychotherapeutic Treatment

Frank Faranda PHD

Frank Faranda

Frank Faranda   CONTACT Frank Faranda, Ph.D. frank@frankfarandaphd.com 330 West 58th Street, #612, New York, NY 10019.

For many decades, cognitive scientists have debated the question of whether mental images exist in the mind or whether they merely appear to exist (Tye, 1991). To those of us not directly involved in this discussion, the question may appear somewhat academic. After all, as Kosslyn (2005) described, if I ask you to tell me the shape of Mickey Mouse’s ears, you will undoubtedly do so through the use of an image in your mind’s eye. In many ways, my understanding of this debate centers on the question of how much we can trust what we see when we look inside. The stark experience of subjectivity present when images are evoked appears to likewise have some bearing on the position images hold in clinical treatment, most specifically in psychodynamic psychotherapy and psychoanalysis. And although the word distrust is perhaps too strong, there does appear to be a subtle discomfort with images dating back to the origins of psychoanalysis (Singer, 1971). And yet, as will become clear from the articles to follow, images and image-based experience are alive and well.

In conceptualizing this issue for Psychoanalytic Inquiry, it was my intention to provide a space for the reader to become acquainted with some of the forms that image-based experience currently takes in psychodynamic treatment and psychoanalysis. What emerges from this discussion, however, has the potential to take the reader beyond a simple recognition of images as a part of psychotherapy process and into realms of philosophy, art, poetry, and neurobiology that offer rich opportunities for therapeutic enhancement.

The issue begins with an article from Rebecca Curtis that traces the use of imagery from Freud and Jung to contemporary authors and theorists. The history of imagery she documents reveals a subtle path of ambivalence surrounding imagery within the psychoanalytic culture. Bringing in her own approach to imagery, Curtis reveals a number of ways in which imagery can be used within a treatment. And as she finishes her article, Curtis discloses a vulnerable moment of the uncanny and its relationship to imagery.

Historically, modern Japanese have been identifying with the spirit of Europeans and Americans, while being involved in the difficult task of maintaining their uniqueness. To understand the motivation of psychiatrists becoming psychoanalysts in Japan, one must consider the era they live in and their new way of life.

The editor of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, Melvin Bornstein, invited a group of Japanese analysts to write articles on how they became psychoanalysts. The task was difficult. It took three years to achieve. It touched on deep emotions and ideas, yet their spirit was present, as seen in this issue that has taken three years to complete.

Dr. Toyoaki Ogawa’s article is revealing and proactive. He writes in a lively and young spirit that, no doubt, reflects qualities of his personality, a strength to learn and investigate, especially about life itself.

Dr. Takayuki Kinugasa was born in Hiroshima after the Pacific War was over. But as he grew older, Dr. Kinugasa began to realize how the A-bomb was boundlessly devastating on human beings, both physically and emotionally. When he was 10 years old, he was involved in a serious accident resulting in a series of traumatic surgeries. This personal incident overlapped the A-bomb tragedy that devastated so many peoples’ lives, including his own father’s, which led to his vocational choice of medicine, psychiatry, and psychoanalysis.

Dr. Kenichiro Okano wrote a very illustrative, illuminating narrative about expectation and goals of psychoanalytic training. He also discusses some important issues around psychoanalytic thinking in modern time.

Dr. Seigen Gon was born as a Korean Japanese. During the period of transition in Japan, Dr. Gon experienced tremendous hardships and agonies. As he was developing his identity of a psychoanalyst, the greater psychoanalytic community itself contributed to addition hardships.

Dr. Akiyoshi Okada’s article describes the history of psychoanalysis in Japan with its transitions during the last half century. The analogy of training of psychoanalysis and that of Japanese martial arts, is well illustrated. Certainly it is culturally bound by nature.

This article focuses on the glorification of violence in the United States and why there is such an attraction to violent images. The data on the impact of violent video games, movies, and television shows tend to focus on whether those images and scenes lead to aggressive behavior, but in this article I highlight the fact that this research indicates that Americans are drawn to images and scenes of violent behavior. The U.S. citizenry does not simply react to what the media companies produce; it chooses video games and shows that contain violence. I address why this is in terms of American exceptionalism and draw the connection between that grandiose image of America and the glorification of violence across a wide range of the American population.

This article addresses the issue of why it is that United States of America glorifies violence and, at the same time, is scared of it, out of proportion to the country’s overwhelming world strength and influence. The article focuses initially on the need to own weapons of mass destruction beyond those needed for sports, including hunting. My psychoanalytic hypothesis suggests that there is a displacement of a fear of being seen by the world as altruistic and, therefore, feminine (castrated and weak); and a hypermasculine defensive façade is often adopted. A history of altruism as reflected in community attitudes is given together with several examples of how altruistic interventions can be very helpful both in schools and in community-wide interventions. The article is the first in a series that will explore altruism as a drive and important in individual analysis beyond its role as an ego defense.

The Dialectics of Psychoanalytic Decision-Making

Frank Summers Ph.D., ABPP

Frank Summers

Frank Summers   Frank Summers, Ph.D., ABPP, is Professor of Clinical Psychiatry and the Behavioral Sciences, Feinberg School of Medicine, Northwestern University, and Supervising and Training Analyst, Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis and the Chicago Center for Psychoanalysis.CONTACT Frank Summers, Ph.D., ABPP franksumphd@gmail.com 333 East Ontario, Suite 4509B, Chicago, IL 60611.

The thesis of this article is that there is no single analytic technique, and psychoanalytic decision-making consists of a dialectical movement among the different possibilities. The aim of the analytic process is to make conscious previously unconscious meaning and motivation and to bring to fruition arrested psychic capabilities, but how that is done is not restricted to any particular technique. Analysts stay silent, ask questions, seek clarification, interpret, and encourage further expression, among other types of interventions. The crux of clinical decision-making for the analyst is to choose which of these various procedures to deploy at any given moment. Each analytic technique deployed means that an alternative is in abeyance and that often means an aspect of the process is neglected. The analytic therapist has a barometer that tells him or her when the neglected part of the process needs to come forth and assert itself. In the dialectics of analytic decision-making, the analytic therapist uses his or her sense of what is being neglected to shift the analytic technique to a different form of intervention. How this dialectic is played out in the analytic process is explored and articulated.

Henry Smith MD

Henry Smith

Henry Smith   CONTACT Henry F. Smith, M.D. henryfsmith@gmail.com 17 Hammond Street, Cambridge, MA 02138.

Despite the fact that psychoanalysts seem to know a confrontation when they see one, surprisingly few have written about it, and even fewer have tried to define it. As several of the authors in this issue point out, it doesn’t appear in the index to the Standard Edition (Freud, 1974) of Freud’s work, nor in the indexes of many other authors that we associate with the concept.

The term, however, has been used in psychoanalysis in a variety of ways. During the first fifty years of the field, it was a simple descriptive term, as in “the ego is confronted with aspects of the id;” everyone knew what it meant from ordinary speech. At some point, it began to take on a more forceful, aggressive connotation, as a specific intervention with especially difficult patients. Finally, beginning in the early 1950s, under the influence of psychoanalysts who had emigrated from Europe, technical procedures were becoming more precise and confrontation began to be mentioned as one of a series of specific technical maneuvers, culminating in Greenson (1964), who designated it as the first stage in a prescribed sequence of interventions in every standard analysis.

Psychoanalysis has changed markedly in the last four decades, however, with many new points of view entering the mainstream in the United States, and different schools, both here and around the world, beginning to talk to one another, out of which have emerged points of agreement, as well as disagreement. But, except in debates between Kernberg (1975) and others on the treatment of borderline patients, that dialogue has rarely included the topic of confrontation.

The time, then, seems right to ask a series of contemporary psychoanalysts from different analytic points of view to give their perspectives on the topic of confrontation and to illustrate those perspectives with clinical material—and it leads to a series of questions:

Is confrontation still a viable term, or has it been discredited as part of an authoritarian past? Do contemporary analysts still confront their patients? How do they define the term? Has it been subsumed by other approaches: careful work from a shared observational surface, for example, or a focus on the interaction between the analyst and the patient, the contemporary scrutiny of enactment, or attention to the analytic field created by the analyst and the patient? How do contemporary Kleinians think of confrontation? Do contemporary ego psychologists differ on the subject from their predecessors?

Do We Glorify Violence in Our Culture? Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Media and Violence

Monisha Nayar-Akhtar PHD

Monisha Nayar-Akhtar

Monisha Nayar-Akhtar   Monisha C. Nayar-Akhtar, Ph.D., is in Private Practice and Faculty, Psychoanalytic Center of Philadelphia and University of Pennsylvania.CONTACT Monisha C. Nayar-Akhtar, Ph.D. monisha_akhtar@hotmail.com 300 E. Lancaster Avenue, Suite 201-B, Wynnewood, PA 19096.

The relationship between media and violence is a complex and perplexing one. A sample of the numerous statistics and studies on this subject illustrates growing developmental implications (as in children who view media violence are more likely to be aggressive), socio-cultural influences (increasing portrayals of real-life violence), as well as political involvement (leaders of a nation asking for the Entertainment Industry to not glorify gun violence). Finally, increasing difficulties in discerning fantasy and real life suggests that at an intrapsychic level, a core function of imaginative play (Winnicott, 1971), an essential ingredient of childhood development, may also be further compromised. Yet, although the escalation of violence in and by the media is ubiquitous and undeniable, it is also true that not all individuals exposed to such violence act upon it, nor do they experience all the developmental challenges as illuminated by research data. Furthermore, significant variations in both cultural and individual expression of violence suggests that other factors more pertinent to intrapsychic functioning, as well as group processes, may also be at play. Last, cyberspace technology has substantially altered the playing field for the depiction of violence with some interesting results. These concerns will be explored in this article.

Eva Papiasvili Ph.D., ABPP

Eva Papiasvili

Eva Papiasvili  

At the Breakfast of the Editors and Guest Editors of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, during the APsaA January 2012 meeting in New York, Dr. Lichtenberg brought up an issue of interpretation in the current diverse psychoanalytic culture. The questions that were posed were: At a time when nonspecific relational aspects of a dyadic system are being emphasized, implicit relational knowing for example, has the role of interpretation changed? If yes, how? What is the role, significant of interpretation and its place in the effect of the verbal symbolic and metaphoric to effect a change? How is interpretation entwined with the spirit of inquiry, growth, openness, resilience, and creativity? Later, as the issue was being further conceptualized, we added the working title: “Interpretation—Then and Now: If, When, and How.” These thoughts and considerations were then sent to the prospective authors—the contributors of this issue—to engage, from whichever angle they find appropriate to their thinking and clinical work.

An ongoing debate concerning clinical and developmental psychoanalytic theory throughout the history of psychoanalysis, involving such issues as multifaceted character of memory, interaction of trauma and fantasy, deficit and conflict, pre-Oedipal and Oedipal, in the development of personality and pathogenesis, has had always significant implications for the view of the psychoanalytic process and the place of interpretation in it, generating various conclusions for successive generations of analysts. The major developments of last 30 years, including contemporary affective, embedded, and developmental neuroscience; infant observation studies; and comparative meta-analyses of clinical studies of the effectiveness of psychoanalytic and other therapies, have profound implications for the subject of interpretation, as well. In a sense, every theoretical debate will ultimately be “tested” in our clinical work, as we interpret (or not) what arises in the clinical situation.

An extraordinary line-up of international authors, many of them major voices of the field of psychoanalysis today, present a colorful rainbow of contemporary approaches to the issue of interpretation, covering the wide map of today’s psychoanalytic world. They address the many questions that were raised at the January 2012 meeting implicitly, if not always explicitly. The inclusion of the wide variety of approaches and angles is one way how we can guard against old and new orthodoxies.

Children and adolescents use a variety of methods to communicate to their analyst, be it verbally, nonverbally, or, as is often the case, in some combination (Sandler, Kennedy, and Tyson, 1980). Unlike adults, whose primary vehicle for communication is language, children turn to other means. They play, using their imaginations and fantasies, employing toys and whatever is available to them in the consulting room; for example, their shoes become cars or planes, a place to hide something they hope (or not) will be found, or in frustration and anger, something to throw. They draw, construct things out of a variety of materials, play games, and, bring their dreams.

It is difficult to talk about the role of dreams in child analysis, without including them in the context of all of the analysis. As Anna Freud (Hampstead Clinic, 1980) said:

Whenever we single out a psychoanalytic concept, and try to study it, we do so in detail, taking that concept alone. … Thus, isolating concepts for study has enormous advantages in learning more about them, but at the same time it falsifies the picture because concepts do not exist in isolation. [p. 193]

A dream is dreamt and then presented within an analytic process, a process that is dynamic and sequential, with an energy, pace, and rhythm where movement is observed and experienced. It is both regressive and progressive, as analyst and child advance toward the analytic aims, be they intermediary or outcome ones (Kennedy and Moran, 1991). There is the micro-process, the one within a single moment or session, and the macro-process, over several sessions or even the entire analysis. Along with the analytic process is the developmental one, where the analyst not only looks back and is concerned with the present, but is also looking forward with an eye toward the future.

Like all concepts, an analytic process does not occur in isolation either, but within the context of a relationship. It is within this relationship that child and analyst begin their journey, with the analyst introducing the child to the aims and methods of treatment, and the two building a working alliance (Fraiberg, 1955; Glenn, 1977; Sandler et al., 1980; Kabcenell, 1993; Novick and Novick, 1998), what Schmukler refers to as a “therapeutic assist.” Karush outlined the multidimensional aspects of the relationship in child analysis, emphasizing the role of transference and its universality (Yanof, 1996). Yet, as with these other analytic concepts, transference exists within a wider context.

Dreams are a fundamental part of our lives that have fascinated and mystified people for centuries and yet there has been little consensus on their origin and function. There are some theories that emphasize the autonomous role of deeper brain structures and see dreaming as an epiphenomenon of rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep without a meaning to decipher. Other theories indicate a role in emotional processing, memory consolidation, or evolutionary roles in preparing people to face threats when awake. Most studies have focused on exploring dreams and their neural correlates in adults, and therefore people still have a limited understanding of dreaming in children. In this review, I discuss some of the past and current findings and theories about the phenomenology, neural underpinnings, and function of dreaming in general with an emphasis on findings in children.

Teach me how to sleep. Catch my nightmares and transform them into dreams.

This is the task that Peter gives to the analyst by asking, through his parents, to start an analytic treatment. It is the same request an Indian girl made to her mother that, according to the legend, originated the invention of the dream catcher. This is an object made of a hoop on which is woven a net that catches the good dream images and filters out the frightening ones through some threads ending with feathers. We follow this image to comment on the clinical section of Christine Anzieu-Premmereur’s work.

Every child analyst knows that, very often, the symptoms that bring a child to analysis signal an environmental difficulty or the partial failure of the psychic functions of one or more family members. It is very important that the analyst’s setting, just like the dream catcher’s main structure, is flexible and broad enough to include all the members of the family.

In this respect, two moments in the clinical account seem significant to us: the explicit request of the analyst for a more active participation of the mother in bringing Peter to the sessions, and the disappearance of the child’s symptoms even before his face-to-face encounter with the analyst.

Something, thus, happened in the first consultation with the parents that enabled them to go back home with a new receptive willingness in relation to their child’s anxieties. The analyst’s dreaming function started to transform the parents’ nightmare—provisionally called Peter—and to convey to them some trust in their own capacity to reestablish a more satisfying relationship with him.

Another particularly therapeutic moment can be identified in the analyst’s capacity to offer to the mother—who was not able to wait for her son in the waiting room—the possibility to enter the playroom. The therapist knows that she needs to take care of the deep loneliness of this mother and her incapacity to play with her child. When Peter asks for a snack and his mother realizes she has not brought it to the session, we can see how this mother, almost unaware, has difficulty taking care of her child’s primary, concrete, and emotional needs. The point here is not a potential human forgetfulness, but how the frustration of the child is not received at all in the mother’s mind. And vice versa, we see that the symmetrical feelings of the mother are projected in the field and end up seeking for some justification in the child’s behavior because of a sense of dissatisfaction. In this flow of evacuations and mutual projections, the analytic work opens up some awareness, but mostly offers an experience of acceptance of the dyad that starts to weave a net for a common dream in the future.

Papiasvili, Ph.D., ABPP, is Senior Clinical Faculty and Supervisor, Doctoral Program in Clinical Psychology at Teachers College, Columbia University in New York; Training and Supervising Analyst, and former Executive Director and Dean, Institute of the Postgraduate Psychoanalytic Society; and Co-Chair for North America, IPA Encyclopedic Dictionary Task Force.136 East 55th Street, # 6A New York, NY 10022 eva.papiasvili@gmail.com

The methodology of psychoanalytic interpretation was originally built on Freud’s view of neuroses as a faulty translation between various systems of experience with different processing codes.

In this article, I attempt to bring this earliest—translational—point of view of the psychoanalytic interpretation up to date: as a configuration of progressively expanding bands of translational connections between and within various experiential systems, including both, the developmentally and dynamically symbolized and non-symbolized mentation.

Translating and interpreting within a thus widened semiotic field of different experiential domains leads potentially to verbally consolidated insight that has been found in recent outome studies to uniquely effect the posttherapy growth. This multidimensional process and its effect is conceptualized as an image/metaphor mediated open work in motion, enhancing unconscious and conscious symbolization and internalized representation, in search of developmentally and dynamically lost connections between the elements of the experiential systems. The clinical vignettes illustrate different aspects of the proposed all-inclusive and eventually internalized multidirectional interpretative configurations with both analyst and patient taking turns as interpreters, under the patient’s authorship.

The image of the Wolf-Man’s drawing of the white wolves in the walnut tree is iconic in the history of psychoanalysis. In this article, the drawing and its creation serve to illustrate not only Freud’s theories concerning the creation of images and imagery, but equally something meaningful about Freud himself. As will become clear, these Freudian theories, drawn from concepts in The Interpretation of Dreams, the papers on metatheory, and a random selection of Freud’s own poetic word images, reveal not only Freud’s interpretive presence but also his personal absence. Challenging Freud's interpretation of the drawing as confirming the Wolf-Man's childhood dream, this article presents potential imagery of the drawing as seen through the lenses of post-Freudian psychoanalytic authors as well as an intriguing quote by art historian Whitney Davis. The author then adds some image creations of her own.

Christine Anzieu-Premmereur M.D., Ph.D. , Denia Barrett MSW and Ruth Karush MD

Ruth Karush

Ruth Karush  

fIn child and adolescent psychoanalysis, the analyst cannot rely on a patient to follow the fundamental rule of free association as part of a shared effort to reach unconscious mental processes. He or she makes inferences about the unconscious from the child’s play, stories, drawings, fantasies, dreams, and the progression of activities during an analytic hour. Of all of these possibilities, dreams may offer the most direct access to the unconscious. The technique of obtaining dream material from young patients depends on the characteristics of childhood and varies with the developmental level of the child. Dream interpretation with children, however, does not differ fundamentally from that with adults. Dreams can be extraordinarily useful in explicating the conflicts of young patients. Thus, it is striking that the analysis of dreams in the psychoanalytic treatment of children is still a relatively neglected area.

In 1927, Anna Freud wrote enthusiastically about the value of dream analysis in child treatment. However, in 1945 she qualified her earlier enthusiasm about the therapeutic value of working with children’s dreams. She said, “Children tell their dreams freely; but without the use of free association, the interpretation of manifest dream content is less fruitful and convincing” (p. 6). It seems to us, however, that dream interpretation can be quite persuasive. We agree with Ablon and Mack (1980) who pointed out that “the potential arbitrariness of an interpretation can be balanced by the child’s subsequent play and verbal response, which may or may not provide confirmation that the analyst is following a fruitful avenue” (p. 205). The clinical articles in the issue, we believe, demonstrate the usefulness of working with dreams. Although the fundamentals of dream interpretation are the same for all ages, the child analyst may have to take active steps to interest his patient in dreams.

In her 1927 paper, Anna Freud wrote:

But there is nothing easier to make the child grasp than dream interpretation. At the first account of a dream, I say, “No dream can make itself out of nothing; it must have fetched every bit from somewhere”—and then I set off with the child in search of its origins.

Marianne Leuzinger-Bohleber   Marianne Leuzinger-Bohleber, Prof. Dr. phil.; Director, The Sigmund Freud Institute, Frankfurt, Germany; Training Analyst, German Psychoanalytic Association; Professor of Psychoanalysis, University of Kassel; Co-Chair for Europe, Research Board, IPA.Dr. Marianne Leuzinger-Bohleber, Direktorin Sigmund-Freud-Institut, Myliusstr. 20, 60323 Frankfurt am Main, Germany, M.Leuzinger-Bohleber@sigmund-freud-institut.de

Trauma is not an unambiguously defined concept. After a discussion of various definitions and different types of trauma, a description is given of short- and long-term outcomes of traumatic experiences. For the treatment of traumatized individuals, and above all, for the interpretation of this kind of experience it is important to note that traumatic memories are subject to some specific psychic transformations. The traumatized self-states are not completely dissociated from the mind’s associative network. Specific interpretive strategies are described that focus on the irreparable break in basic trust, the need to control relationships, the importance of the reconstruction of the trauma, the restoring of the paralyzed agency of the traumatized self, and the particular attention that must be paid to enactments in the treatment. In the final part, a new understanding of memory in so-called Embodied Cognitive Science is described. Memory is no longer a retrieval of stored knowledge in the brain, but a function of the entire organism, the product of complex, dynamic recategorization and invariably embodied interactive processes. By way of a clinical example, the manner is illustrated in which this new conception provides an alternative explanation as to how traumatic memories function, and how the latter are understood in psychoanalytic treatment.

This article explores time utilizing analytic process between a young man who is dramatically symptomatic and his analyst. In the course of the play, the minds of each of his parents are revealed to be present reflecting earlier, concomitant, and unsolvable dilemmas that they contain. Nachtraglichkeit has been translated into English as deferred action or afterwardness, and in French as apres-coup, literally after-blow. Freud used the word initially to describe how sexually charged encounters in childhood produce traumatic effects after the fact, when puberty ascribes new meanings to these memories. In this article, I consider a greatly expanded, radicalized view of nachtraglichkeit as encompassing any enactment or insight that generates an experience of retrospective disorganization. I consider both a traumatic, destructive dimension of nachtraglichkeit and an everyday, expansive dimension of nachtraglichkeit, such as emerges in the clinical situation, in which small-scale disorganizations and reorganizations of the past allow for an enlarged sense of self and world. In considering nachtraglichkeit from the everyday, developmental dimension, I consider how the phenomenon often emerges out of an expanded field of inquiry formed of two minds elaborating backwards around the experiences of one.

According to Green, psychoanalysts have lost the fundamental complexity of Freudian temporality and act as if time proceeded linearly from past to present to future. The debate over here-and-now transference interpretations, as opposed to reconstruction, disguises just such a reductive linearity. Two types of time existed for Green. The first takes fact into account; the second makes use of the regression afforded by sleep to ignore the passage of time. Freud was not talking about a regression to a reconstituted past, which would bring one back to linearity, but a regression to outdated means of expression and to images that represent wishes, as opposed to words that convey those wishes.

Any object relation brings with it a relation to time—to past, present and future. Complementarily, any relation to time carries with it a corresponding relation to a set of objects. Temporal relations and object relations beget and inform each other. Patients who mean to retreat from objects are faced with the more daunting problem of having to retreat from time itself. Dreams create unique opportunities and challenges for the child and adolescent psychoanalyst. Epilogue: Confrontation in Psychoanalysis

Henry Smith MD

Henry Smith

Henry Smith   CONTACT Henry F. Smith, M.D. henryfsmith@gmail.com 17 Hammond Street, Cambridge, MA 02138.

Given the controversial history of the concept of confrontation, it is only natural that our five authors are all talking about somewhat different conceptions of the term. I think they can be divided into three main types: (1) confrontation as an intrinsic part of any encounter between one person and another, (2) confrontation as a specific technical maneuver, and (3) confrontation as an attitude on the part of the analyst (or the patient) based on anger, aggression, and blame. No longer does anyone seem to think of confrontation as an ordinary descriptive term, as it was used during the first half of the last century. Let us take the three types one at a time.

In terms of the first conception, Ferro and Civitarese, who ultimately settle on a somewhat different point of view, note the ubiquity of confrontation when they comment, “A wider conception, on the other hand, would tend to take account of the degree of confrontation implicit in any intervention” (p. 307). More explicitly, both LaFarge, in her beautifully self-observed clinical presentation, and I explore the presence of confrontation in all analytic dialogue and its role in the enactments that result from the encounter with another person.

Notice that highlighting the element of confrontation in all dialogue does effectively return confrontation to its original descriptive meaning. One does not need a psychoanalytic dictionary to know what is meant by the confrontation between two strangers. And that ordinariness may have some advantages in focusing the analyst and the patient on other aspects of psychoanalytic process, such as the empathic tracing of the patient’s experience, the examination of the interaction from an immersion in the enactments that result, the building of representations, or listening to the messages from the analytic field and intervening from within that field. In other words, if we refrain from collapsing the conceptualization of what we are doing into a series of simple technical devices, then we are necessarily thrown into examining the encounter with the other in one form or another and into trying to observe what is actually happening within both individuals in the consulting room. That encounter starts as a confrontation between two strangers.

Marilyn Nissim-Sabat PHD

Marilyn Nissim-Sabat

Marilyn Nissim-Sabat   Marilyn Nissim-Sabat, Ph.D., is Professor Emeritus, Philosophy Department, Lewis University; Psychodynamic Therapist in Private Practice; and Author of Neither Victim nor Survivor: Thinking Toward a New Humanity (Lexington, 2009).CONTACT Marilyn Nissim-Sabat, Ph.D. nissimma@hotmail.com 4747 S. The theme of this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry opens up an important field of inquiry. There is abundant and clear evidence that violence is glorified in our culture, and around the world as well. The critically important question is: Why is violence glorified, and how can we prevent both violence and its glorification? These issues are addressed in this article in the form of the following question: How is it that so many people in our culture conclude that they do not have other, nonviolent, nonaddictive options for meeting their profound human need for the feeling of well-being? This question is addressed here through an investigation of the role of the relationship between the options available to people and the actual choices that they make. I show that endemic failure to address this options-to-choice relationship in psychoanalysis, developmental psychology, and philosophy is a factor in ongoing controversies in psychoanalytic theory and clinical theory as well as in philosophical psychology. I show further that (a) this failure has been a factor in our inability to understand and prevent violence, and (b) a phenomenological philosophical framework for psychoanalysis can point the way to greater insight into the problem of violence and its prevention.

In this article, I examine the impact of extensive modification of the body on the temporal link, which is an important feature of human identity, as it provides continuity between different representations of the self over time. I illustrate this with a case of a young boy who underwent sex reassignment surgery in late adolescence after the artificial suspension of puberty through sex hormones. I argue that when hormones are used in this way, one can observe in some cases not only the desired suspension of physical time during which the body’s given biological trajectory is artificially halted, but also of psychological time. In some instances, this biological and psychic detour can result in a marked distortion in the young person’s relationship to time and impacts on their psychological adaptation following surgery.

This article traces four modes of traumatic testimony that are distinguished from one another in the degree of the psychic motility they succeed to form in relation to traumatic memories: the metaphoric, the metonymic, the excessive-psychotic, and the Muselmann-psychotic modes of testimony. While the metaphoric mode is characterized by the simultaneous holding of the position of the victim (the experiencing I) and the position of the witness (the narrating I), the other three modes are gradually declining in their capacity to hold the traumatic memories in mind in a way that allows for transformation and healing. These four modes are illustrated through a close reading of various testimonies suggesting that the core of the psychoanalytic treatment of trauma lies in the attempt to enable the crucial shift from the metonymic, the excessive, and the Muselmann modes of testimony to the metaphoric one, which is the only force that can turn the traumatic lacuna into a creative force.

In basic psychoanalytic theory of technique, interpretation and insight reveal the latent content beneath the manifest appearance of symptoms, character pathology, and disturbed irrational behavior. The understanding of the neutrality and objectivity of the analyst, however, has been modified with new formulations of interpersonal, intersubjective influence and dyadic unconscious communication. Transference is often regarded as coconstructed in the present in a transference-countertransference field, emphasizing the analytic relationship and experience as a two-person analytic process. Nevertheless, the analyst is capable of good enough objectivity and neutrality for analytic work. Countertransference interpretation expands insight into the patient, as well as the analyst. Interpretation is not only resisted, but is reinterpreted by the analytic dyad with gradual partial insight and integration. The infantile unconscious, genetic interpretation, and reconstruction are often devalued in some object relations frameworks. A clinical vignette illustrates the continued importance of the past in the present without neglect of current determinants and perspectives. While integrating newer considerations of the two-person analytic field, interpretation and insight into the dynamic unconscious are here regarded as the sine qua non of psychoanalysis.

“Why psychoanalysis? How do Japanese get to know psychoanalysis?” These questions were given at the interview on my applying to Tavistock Clinic, when I introduced myself as already accepted by the Institute of Psychoanalysis in London. It was in 1998. Two years later, our year group, newly progressed to the formal candidate starting the seminars at the Institute, was invited to Freud Museum as a part of the introductory events by the Institute. There, the director told us that Freud himself had an ambition and hope to spread his psychoanalysis into Japan. How can we integrate the discrepancy between those sincere questions and Freud’s ambition? Reflecting on recent prevalence in Psychoanalytic Community in terms of Go to the East, one might say that heading for the East is influenced by the trend in the world economy, which is no more than marketing and politics. Of course, as fellows of psychoanalysis, we would see and could also comprehend that heading for the East is definitely the sincere interest to achieve further understanding of human psyche in depth by relating each other. Because psychoanalysis is a way to understand one’s own, by creating an understanding in depth, through the analytic, i.e., unconscious-oriented mutual communication with a psychoanalyst. Therefore, it is inevitable for both of us, the East and the West, to know each other, so far as pursuing our sincere wish to comprehend what kind of invisible unconscious reservation might be transparent in one’s own cultural context.

As noted in the introduction, psychoanalysis is intellectually introduced to Japan in the 1910s, the era of Imperialism. However, once trying to comprehend and conduct psychoanalysis in terms of the formal clinical practice as well as becoming a psychoanalyst, it has taken several decades to overcome. To illustrate the reality of our struggling, Dr. Ogura and I decided to add articles by Drs. Takeo Doi and Tetsuro Takahashi. Like the other six authors (and me, too, who studied the dynamic psychiatry at Menninger, and later on, trained at the Institute of Psychoanalysis in London), we have moved quite a lot, not just because of geographical reasons. Why did it happen? Some articles illustrate the devastated (and inevitably traumatized) scene after the Second World War, including the atomic bombing, and the racial discrepancy within Far Eastern Nations. In a way, they were influenced by the war trauma in the history, more or less, which also indicates the disturbance by the encounter, as Japan closed its doors against almost all of foreign countries for more than two hundred years, until the late 19th century and it was, in a way, penetrated when Black Ships (Western vessels arriving in Japan) came from the United States in the middle of the 19th century. Then, the first modernization in Japan began to emulate the method of Western nations such as England, Germany, and France. However, its excessive way resulted in World War II, which caused huge kinds of turmoil and confusion. Thinking of this kind of false identification to the new object, it might be acted in the field of psychoanalysis, too. This time, it resulted in Amsterdam Shock, mentioned in some articles.

The purpose of my article is to face up to, and to know more, about the depth-psychology of jealousy, which constitutes a part of my personal history of taking the path to becoming a psychiatrist and choosing to specialize in psychoanalysis. In other words, it is closely related to my experience of having achieved success, in a sense, in my early 20s, which made me the object of jealously, and experiencing the anxiety and fear that comes from being a total unknown who becomes one of “the Beatles of Japan.” I became something I wanted to be, but I was also scared of being scolded by God. I was expelled, at least psychologically, from Japan. I fled to London and underwent psychoanalysis. I desperately wanted to learn exactly what was happening to me, reading the story that was repeated in our hearts, in our fantasies, in my songs, and also in reality. In the course of both undergoing and studying psychoanalysis, I encountered something that was the last thing I wanted to recognize: my own sense of jealousy. I then concluded that my songs are created for you—that special someone who is there. They are not in any way created for someone to become just famous or just to please someone jealous.

This is an account of a personal journey from a foreigner in Japan to a psychoanalyst. This article proposes a paradigm shift from an emphasis on explanation to a concentration on exploration as a way of resolving some problems related to interpretation in analytic treatment. Specifically, it is argued that psychoanalysis can meaningfully proceed by connecting the internal psychological world to current functioning without depending upon connections to the past. Dreams play a central role in the process of working through emotional experiences. When dream work fails to perform this function, the capacity to form symbols is affected. The ability to dream and create representations well-organized enough to be remembered is associated with good regulation of emotions and symbolization. Some children do not develop these abilities, due to difficulties in containing disorganized experiences, including traumatic ones. The first sessions with a five-year-old boy suffering from night terrors, and the parallel work with his parents, show how the role of maternal containment is essential for developing this capacity. In addition to its function of wish fulfillment, dreaming is a process of representation that fills the void of nonrepresentation associated with traumatic experiences of presymbolic origin.

This article reviews much of the history of the use of imagery from Breuer and Freud, Jung, Ferenczi to Reyher, Singer, Desoille, Assagioli, Beck, and Ahsen. In addition, I present my theoretical and clinical perspectives on the use of imagery in psychoanalysis. My own work involves using the Gestalt technique of asking a patient to become the person or object in a dream or the mind’s eye, often with powerful results.
